articles.title_orig: Nvidia earnings live updates: Wall Street braces for first report since Huang's ouster
articles.title_zh: Nvidia earnings live updates: Wall Street braces for first report since Huang's ouster
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

articles.title_orig: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.title_zh: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.content_orig:

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila , the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un .
Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports.
A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration’s request of $30.1 billion, “the urgent need for this investment became undeniable.” That’s when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop.
The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure.
Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
Trump’s pick to lead the Navy focuses on shipbuilding in his opening statements
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told senators at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that he’ll focus on revitalizing shipbuilding in an effort to expand the nation’s fleet of warships.
But Cao avoided potentially thorny topics that are likely to come up before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Those include the Iran war, the recent firings of Navy admirals and the waiver Cao will need from Congress to become Navy secretary because he left active duty less than seven years ago.
Cao also spoke of his biography, which includes fleeing Vietnam with his family right before the fall of Saigon in the 1970s. He also focused on his 25 years of service in the Navy.
“I spent my entire adult life serving in the United States Navy special operations community with multiple combat deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia,” Cao said.
Bipartisan concerns arise over forces being ‘stretched thin’ during Navy secretary hearing
Despite deep divisions over the Iran war, the Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee voiced a unified concern over the impact the ongoing military operation and internal issues at the Department of Defense have had on the U.S. Navy.
“Our sailors and Marines are our greatest asset, but they cannot sustain an increasingly demanding operational tempo without adequate support,” GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, the committee chair, said during his opening statement.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Jack Reed, echoed his worry, saying that “disruption” from high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, “sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines.”
Confirmation hearing for Trump’s nominee to lead the US Navy gets underway
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, appeared Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee as he seeks the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. It’s the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Cao also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
ASEAN-US dinner menu features American surf and turf
The main course was a pairing of U.S. beef tenderloin and lobster tail, served with a truffle potato puree, glazed baby carrots, oyster mushrooms and a wine sauce, according to details shared by the White House.
Courses before the main included ratatouille, goose liver mousse and burrata cheese salad with heirloom tomatoes, walnuts, balsamic glaze and olive oil.
Chocolate-covered cake with roasted almonds and salted caramel ice cream was served for dessert.
Trump’s pick for Navy secretary likely to face Iran war questions during confirmation hearing
He’s scheduled to testify before a Senate committee Tuesday, the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
Cao will face the current Congress, with Republicans still in charge. But he’s likely to face intense scrutiny from Democrats over aspects of the Iran war, including major damage to the service’s 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, as well as the recent firings of Navy officials.
Trump could meet Imelda Marcos during summit in Philippines
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion between Trump and an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet-set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘Please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
US and Thailand sign joint statement affirming terms of forthcoming trade deal
At a brief signing ceremony in Manila, Trump said Thailand has agreed to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove “substantial” nontariff barriers on American automobiles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.
Trump said Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products and “that makes our farmers very happy.”
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said there’s still “a little more to do” before the agreement itself is finalized and that it should be “ready for us to sign real soon.”
Trump still talking about possible meetings with Russia, North Korea leaders
Trump says North Korea’s leader would like to meet with him in China later this week. And he’s open to sitting down with Russian President Vladimir Putin, too.
But so far, it appears neither meeting has been arranged.
Trump landed in the Philippines on Tuesday for talks with Asia-Pacific leaders. On Thursday, he’s due in Shenzhen, China, for more talks, including a historic three-way confab with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“We’ll see what happens,” Trump said in Manila when reporters asked about North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip Ahead of Nvidia Earnings — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_zh: Wall St falls before Nvidia earnings in key AI test; Huang says open to return
articles.content_orig:
In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I  would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement.
Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO, putting together an online petition with more than 180,000 signatures.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang, Nvidia's founder, admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had a liason with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang also reportedly had romances with employees at Nvidia.
Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Its board of directors said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Here is the entire statement from Huang:
Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry  colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the  greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it  into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor.  Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I  love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious  mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my  mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent  investigation.
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my  return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Correction: Jensen Huang is the former CEO of Nvidia. His title was misstated in a headline on an earlier version of this article.

articles.title_zh: iCloud, App Store, and other Apple services hit by ongoing outage
articles.content_orig:
Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.
Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.
Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.
Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.
Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.
Users are reporting unexpected iCloud sign-outs on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures or unknown errors when trying to sign back in.
I noticed it when I was trying to setup an old iPad and it gave an error that it couldn't connect to activation servers, then a minute later, iCloud Drive on my PC threw an error that it couldn't sync.
Of course, the worthless Apple System Status was all lit up green.
Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect .
The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage .
Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
For years, Ukraine has had a bull’s-eye on the only bridge linking the occupied Crimean Peninsula to Russia.
After Moscow used Crimea as a springboard to launch its all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Kyiv bombed the bridge that year with explosives hidden in a truck. The next year, Ukraine attacked it with unmanned naval vessels . Two years after that, it dispatched covert operatives to try to bring the bridge down by planting explosives on undersea support pillars.
The 12-mile-long structure, the Kerch Strait Bridge, survived it all, a powerful if scarred symbol of Moscow’s control of Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014 . But before dawn on Tuesday, Ukraine struck its biggest blow yet, sending a significant section of the bridge into the sea after a series of drone and missile attacks.
In a statement about the bridge, the Ukrainian military command said, “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever.’”
“Now,” the statement added, “part of the structure lies in the water.”
The Ukrainian government released photographs and video documenting the attack and aftermath. The New York Times also verified social media video showing the collapse of a central span of the bridge used for vehicle traffic.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.title_zh: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.content_orig:
The Civilization and XCOM developer is shrinking as a new XCOM game has missed a development milestone, according to Bloomberg
Take-Two Interactive $TTWO 's Firaxis Games cut roughly 60 jobs on Tuesday, about one-third of the studio's workforce, according to Bloomberg .
A spokesperson from 2K Games, the Take-Two imprint that oversees Firaxis, verified that Heather Hazen, who heads the studio, is departing, according to Bloomberg. The Maryland-based studio makes the Civilization and XCOM franchises.
"Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength — designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," the spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis."
The spokesperson described Hazen’s exit as a planned handover, according to Game Developer . “With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start,” the spokesperson said, according to Game Developer.
Firaxis has been working on a new XCOM title that ran into development problems and fell short of an important milestone this summer, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing unnamed people, said work on the game will go on, though the cuts could bring major changes to it.
“Civilization VII,” the studio’s latest title, came out last year to a lukewarm response and has been patched repeatedly since, according to Bloomberg. The game holds a 51% positive user rating on Steam, according to Kotaku .
The layoffs land just two days prior to “Grand Theft Auto VI” hitting the market, according to Bloomberg. Rockstar, a separate Take-Two label, develops and publishes that game.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Breaks Silence, Signals Willingness to Return as Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Breaks Silence, Signals Willingness to Return as Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang finally addressed his resignation publicly — and he'd be happy to undo it if invited back.
In his statement, Huang said he owned his "mistakes completely" and that he was cooperating with an internal investigation.
The statement adds new pressure to Nvidia's board and interim leadership hours before the company reports quarterly earnings after the closing bell.
Here's what business and tech leaders and personalities are saying about Huang's statement:
Kalanick, who's pushed publicly for Huang to be reinstated, celebrated the statement on X. The Uber cofounder was famously pushed out of his own company in 2017.
"Let's bring Jensen back!!! LFG," he wrote .
Nvidia's board could now face increased pressure, Ives and his colleagues wrote in a research note for Yorkville Ives.
"Clearly Jensen wants to come back as CEO, and the statement moves the fight from a petition to the board," the note reads.
The research note said Nvidia's bylaws allow a critical mass of shareholders to call a special meeting — and with President Donald Trump , Elon Musk, and many employees on board, "that coalition is no longer unthinkable."
But the fight over Nvidia's next CEO will play out in Washington, where federal authorities will want an outsider and compliance with export controls, according to Yorkville Ives' note.
"The board's decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a President open to his return and a Treasury Secretary demanding an outsider," the note says.
On X, Ives posted, "This could be next step in Nvidia saga."
Huang's got a fan with at least one of the All-In Podcast hosts.
"Bring @JensenHuang back 🫡," Calacanis posted .
Baker, an Nvidia shareholder who co-wrote a letter to its board urging it not to rush to judgment with its CEO search, praised Huang as an "exceptional" CEO during an interview with CNBC's Sara Eisen on "Squawk on the Street."
Huang put out his statement moments before Baker appeared on TV — and Baker was glad to see Huang say he would cooperate with investigations.
"I think this is all good," he said on CNBC. "I think this is good for America. I think this is good for Nvidia."
Baker said he wanted to see Huang back at Nvidia.
"America loves comebacks and second chances and I would like to see Jensen, if he is cleared of these charges, given a second chance as to be the CEO of Nvidia," Baker said.

articles.title_orig: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.title_zh: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science . "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui , a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

articles.title_orig: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.title_zh: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.content_orig:
Published 17 November 2026 3:32pm
Share this with family and friends
The Hungarian prime minister has called for resignations from opposing political parties after authorities recovered $US19.5 million ($28.9 million) in cash while investigating bribery claims against a former government minister.
Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who defeated former prime minister Viktor Orbán in an April election and pledged to investigate alleged corruption during Orbán's long tenure, said the scandal was just the "tip of the iceberg" and that his anti-corruption drive would continue.
On Friday, authorities recovered the cash — some buried in forests or hidden in farm buildings and warehouses — as part of a bribery investigation into Miklós Seszták, a minister under Orbán. The money found was a mixture of Hungarian forints, euros and US dollars.
The cash find is the latest in a series of graft investigations into officials who served under Orbán. Another former minister and a former central bank chief have been arrested over graft accusations — which they deny.
Two recent polls show Magyar’s Tisza party has widened its lead over Orbán's Fidesz since September.

"If you have a shred of decency left in you, I ask that you be brave and apologise to the Hungarian people, and then return your mandates," Magyar said during a fiery speech in parliament, before 2027 budget discussions.
Fidesz wrote in a Facebook post that it hoped Seszták was not connected to the cash.
Seszták, Orbán’s development minister from 2014 to 2018, has denied wrongdoing. Orbán has denied allegations of corruption.
Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka said any abuse of public money was unacceptable and an independent court should deliver a verdict.
Bence Rétvári, a member of Fidesz’s former coalition partner Christian Democrats, told parliament it rejected being condemned by Magyar "based on collective sin".
But many Hungarians were appalled by the footage showing vast piles of cash laid out by authorities during the probe, at a time when the economy is struggling to recover from years of stagnation.
"I was stunned when I saw all those billions of forints that were dug up from the forests. It’s almost as if the country were in a science fiction story," Budapest resident Nora Szucs said.
A survey published by the 21 Research Centre on Monday showed that Tisza had 65 per cent support among decided voters, up from 60 per cent in September. Fidesz stood at 24 per cent, down from 26 per cent.
Pollster Median, which correctly predicted the outcome of the April election, said in a survey last week that Tisza’s support rose to 55 per cent from 54 per cent in September, while Fidesz dropped to 16 per cent from 22 per cent two months earlier.

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

articles.title_orig: Iran targets US sites in Bahrain after 2-month pause
articles.title_zh: Iran targets US sites in Bahrain after 2-month pause
articles.content_orig:
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said Tuesday that mediation efforts between the U.S. and Iran were continuing and a meeting with the Iranian side would be held later in the day to exchange views on proposals under discussion.
He warned any escalation on the ground posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
Earlier, President Trump said Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if it follows through on its reported desire to set off a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C. — a claim denied by Iranian officials .
Mr. Trump made the remark after being quizzed by reporters about whether there was an imminent threat to Washington from Iran.
"I hope it's not. But we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," said Trump, who was meeting with leaders of Japan, India and Australia in the Philippines.
The Iran-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen said it carried out successful drone strikes Tuesday on the Saudi East-West pipeline.
Pumping Station No. 9, west of Riyadh, was allegedly targeted in two phases with three one-way attack drones, the Houthis said. They then targeted Pumping Station No. 8 with two drones. The Houthis claimed they made "precise and direct" hits on the pumping stations.
The Saudis had earlier said they shot down a Houthi drone near Riyadh but it was unclear if it was related to the attack on the East-West pipeline.
The pipeline, which is comprised of 11 pumping stations, was previously targeted in a drone attack on Sept. 11, which knocked out the line for nearly two weeks. That attack was blamed on Iran-backed rebel groups located in northern Iraq.
The pipeline gives the Saudis a way to avoid the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait and instead take oil north in the Red Sea out of the Suez Canal. The 750-mile pipeline, built in the 1980s, consists of two separate pipes carrying a maximum capacity of 7 million barrels of oil per day.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthi militia intercepted and shot down a drone near Riyadh on Tuesday, the spokesperson for the group, Col. Turki Al-Malki, said on X.
The Houthis have regularly fired one-way attack drones at Riyadh since the civil war in Yemen restarted this summer. The Houthis have been fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni forces aligned with the internationally recognized government.
This was the fourth straight day the Houthis had fired attack drones into Saudi Arabia, but all of them were intercepted, according to the coalition. The Saudi coalition said it intercepted two drones in the Mecca and Riyadh regions on Monday as well as four separate Houthi drone attacks across the country on Sunday.
Iranian authorities have intensified their repression of the country's population in response to the Middle East war, which began weeks after their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests killed thousands of people , Amnesty International said on Tuesday.
An internet blackout imposed at the time of the crackdown on Jan. 8 and 9 and the scale of the casualties meant it was not yet possible for the group to quantify the number of people killed, Amnesty's lead Iran researcher, Raha Bahreini, said.
But she told AFP in an interview that "there is no doubt that thousands were massacred in less than 48 hours."
She added that the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, "with Iranians still reeling from the January massacres, created a horrific situation for the people in the country."
"The authorities used the cover of wartime conditions to intensify repression," she said.
Bahreini lamented the international community had shifted its attention away from the Iranian people to the geopolitical consequences of the conflict.
"The massacres that took place in January, which should have moved then global consciousness, have faded away from attention," she said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi slammed reports that his country was targeting Washington, D.C., with chemical weapons or building missiles under dams, blaming the reports on Israel.
"In the past 72 hours, pro-Israel media have 'reported' that Iran is supposedly plotting to use chemical weapons in DC while building missile bases under dams. RUBBISH," Araghchi wrote on X .
CNN reported that Iran could be developing plans to target administration officials with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington. According to sources cited by CNN, Tehran's planning is, for now, "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack."
Separately, The New York Times reported that Iran's network of dams might be cover for underground missile development.
In his social media post, Araghchi also invoked the misguided U.S. assertion of there being weapons of mass destruction in Iraq as cause for invading that country in 2003 .
"Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it," Araghchi said Tuesday. "Nobody is buying it."
Araghchi has been one of the most important members of negotiations between the U.S. and Iran over a lasting peace deal.
The United States on Tuesday carried out several attacks on Iran's southern Island of Qeshm, located in the Strait of Hormuz, a local Iranian official said.
"The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas," said Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of the southern province of Hormozgan, quoted by the official IRNA news agency.
There was no immediate confirmation of an attack by the United States.
Qeshm Island has been a regular target of strikes by the U.S. throughout the war. Most of them have been categorized as "defensive" attacks targeting drone or missile launch equipment. The U.S. acknowledged Iran fired multiple one-way attack drones toward Bahrain, but said they were all shot down.
A powerful Iran-backed armed group in Iraq vowed on Tuesday to confront government forces if they try to enter its main stronghold near Baghdad, denying allegations it is smuggling oil from the area.
The standoff between Kataib Hezbollah and Iraqi authorities is shaping up to be the first major test of the new government's resolve to disarm nonstate armed groups.
Abu Taleb al-Saidi of Kataib Hezbollah made the comments a day after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said security forces would enter Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad in Babil province, later this week. Local media reported the group had until Friday to leave.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq's most powerful armed groups, wields considerable influence in Jurf al-Sakhar and has maintained an armed presence there for more than a decade.
The planned move by al-Zaidi is part of his push to disarm powerful Iran-backed groups by mid-2027. The move by the rival sides raises alarms of internal Shiite fighting that has been mostly avoided since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that removed Saddam Hussein from power.
Iran's navy claimed a third oil tanker struck a sea mine near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday after trying to use shipping lanes declared safe and open by the United States, but which Iranian authorities have repeatedly warned mariners against using.
The semi-official Fars news agency cited the Iranian Army Navy as saying the third "offending" tanker "caught fire after striking a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz."
"Our message is clear: the Strait of Hormuz is closed. Safe passage requires coordination with the Iranian Armed Forces, transit through designated safe zones, and having navigation systems switched on," the Fars report cited the navy as saying.
Iran has made claims of ships striking sea mines in and around the southern Strait of Hormuz for weeks, without offering evidence. articles.content_orig:
Various systems at the National Security Agency (NSA) experienced "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" on Tuesday, a U.S. official told Fox News.
"While some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues," the official added. "NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."
A prior Fox News Digital report also said the NSA had not lost critical communications capabilities as a result of the issue.
The House Homeland Security Committee will hold its annual "Worldwide Threats" hearing on Wednesday morning at 10 a.m. ET.
At that hearing, Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin will likely face heavy questioning about the issues at the NSA, as well as the many other tech outages over the last several days.
Fox News' Jennifer Griffin contributed to this post.
Upon entering the sixth day of sustained tech disruptions, U.S. lawmakers have begun to call on Trump administration officials to hold briefings with Congress and share what they know thus far.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the favorite to become House Speaker next year, said Tuesday that the outages are "troubling" and that it's "unclear if it’s all infrastructure related or whether there’s some malignant activity."
"I think it’s too premature to know in the absence of a high level briefing for the Gang of Eight," the New York lawmaker said.
The Gang of Eight is a colloquial term for a group of eight top congressional leaders who are briefed by the executive branch on highly classified intelligence matters. The group includes the Speaker of the House, the House Minority Leader, the Senate Majority Leader, the Senate Minority Leader, and the chairs and ranking minority members of both the House and Senate intelligence committees.
"I think we’ve gotten to a point where we need a bicameral briefing, a briefing for House members, Democrats and Republicans , and a briefing for Senate members, Democrats and Republicans about all of these developments that have taken place within the last week or so," Jeffries added.
Outgoing Republican Reps. Nancy Mace of South Carolina and Mike Lawler of New York also called for greater transparency from the administration.
"Five major outages in less than a week. Microsoft. Workday. The FAA. Major banks. Now the NSA's classified communications network. Congress needs to be briefed immediately. The American people deserve answers about what's going on," Mace said.
Lawler referenced a cyberattack on nearly 200 websites reported Tuesday by Reuters in his call for congressional briefings.
"Given today’s cyberattack, coupled with the FAA ground-stops, banking failures, and Microsoft outage, it’s imperative the administration immediately brief Congress on the exact nature of the problem, so that we can have an all of government response," Lawler said in a post on social media. "While some of this may be coincidental, it is clear we must take cybersecurity and the nefarious use of AI seriously — and act without delay."
Meanwhile, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who called for the resignation of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the FAA ground stop, has touted her state's cyber defense capabilities.
"When I first became governor, I was not confident in our response time or our ability to manage complex crises that this new technologically dependent age calls upon us," Hochul said Tuesday during a press conference.
She continued: "So I really beefed up. I found the top cybersecurity expert in the country, hired that individual. He built an entire team. I've been involved in their tabletop exercises where we game out every possible scenario, doomsday scenarios and how we respond. And we've done this with the city as well."
Google said Tuesday afternoon that it sees no evidence of a "broad Gmail service disruption," despite sustained reports of users struggling to receive emails.
"Our teams monitor service health closely, and real-time status updates are always available on the Google Workspace Status Dashboard," a Google spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
That dashboard currently shows no problems with Gmail or the rest of Google's suite of productivity apps.
Apple's iCloud — where millions of users store photos, documents and other personal data — is seeing a spike in user-reported login issues Tuesday, according to outage tracker Downdetector.
Users have also said they've been unable to reliably access Apple Pay, Apple Music, Apple Card and the App Store.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Multiple sources have confirmed to Fox News that an internal communications system at the National Security Agency (NSA) was at least partially down on Tuesday morning.
A source on Capitol Hill told Fox News "this is just routine patching of systems" at the NSA.
Another source said the NSA is handling it and that because the outage is not believed to be caused by a cyberattack, the Department of Homeland Security and other agencies responsible for cyber protection are not involved.
A third person familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that the NSA staggered arrival times for personnel to prevent tens of thousands of employees from logging in simultaneously, buying officials time to resolve the disruption.
Fox News Digital also learned that there has been "no loss of critical communications" because the NSA has "plenty of backup facilities."
Fox News Digital's Katelyn Caralle and Morgan Phillips contributed to this post. Read more here .
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) will stop installing new routers across its thousands of telecommunications hubs throughout the country after the agency was forced to ground all U.S. flights last week.
Fox Business Network confirmed the news Tuesday. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report the development.
L3Harris, the contractor responsible for maintaining the decades-old FAA telecommunications infrastructure , installed a new router at a radio transmitter site in Arkansas on Friday.
Officials said this new router began sending out too many connection signals at once, overwhelming the network and interfering with the ability for air traffic controllers to communicate with airplanes in the sky. This is what led to the FAA issuing the ground stop.
In addition to pausing new router installation, the FAA has disabled the functionality believed to be the initial cause of Friday’s disruption on more than 60 similar routers.
Fox Business Network's Grady Trimble contributed to this post.
After reports that some Charles Schwab customers couldn't log into their accounts on Tuesday, the financial services company revealed there was a "brief webpage loading issue" that has since been resolved.
"Trading remained available, and clients could access their accounts at schwab.com/login or through the Schwab Mobile app. We apologize for the inconvenience," Schwab told Fox News in a statement.
Schwab was only the latest bank or brokerage firm to suffer serious technical issues. Most notably, JPMorgan Chase's systems were down for hours on Monday, leaving customers unable to withdraw money or access their accounts.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News on Monday that artificial intelligence could be at least partly to blame for the recent wave of breakdowns across critical digital systems Americans rely on daily to travel and work.
Mullin told "Hannity" host Sean Hannity that the theory that AI, or "super intelligence" (SI), contributed to the cascading service failures came up during a briefing with a prominent technology expert.
"These programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in and it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one t

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang’s family shaped Nvidia’s Singapore dealings
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang’s family shaped Nvidia’s Singapore dealings
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang speaks during GTC Berlin on October 21, 2026.
Nvidia's board has reportedly and wisely closed the door on Jensen Huang’s return, barely a week after boardroom pressure pushed him to resign as chief executive. A dubious outside campaign is still trying to pry it open. Tech leaders like SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Y Combinator’s Garry Tan have signed a petition demanding his reinstatement, while financier shareholders Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged Nvidia's board via letter to “avoid a rush to replace Jensen.”
That door should stay shut. Over 33 years, Huang built the company at the center of the AI era, but in our view, his conduct nevertheless made his position untenable. He misled directors about undisclosed relationships and oversaw a firm no one could check—a breakdown in trust that was magnified in China, where he advocated loosening export controls even as restricted chips reached Chinese military units and a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network.
The political push to restore him rests on the billions his most prominent advocates have riding on his customer-financing web and on misleading geopolitical spin, at the expense of genuine shareholder concerns and national defense.
In the spirit of the transparency we ask of Huang’s advocates, we note that our upcoming book, When Machines Act: The Promise and Peril of Our Agentic AI Future , includes Huang’s own words, drawn from his commentary at our Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute CEO forums.
For 13 months , Huang maintained through spokespeople that his ties to Alice Huang, head of major customer Megaspeed, were strictly business. Only after the Financial Times reported Washington’s concerns about her did the Nvidia CEO confess the affair to general counsel Tim Teter. Even then, he assured Teter, who spoke with the board, that there had been no others. Four days later, the New York Times uncovered a second affair .
The Megaspeed entanglement posed a textbook conflict of interest. Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of scarce processors and is under federal investigation , and Nvidia's own code of conduct flags personal relationships as a conflict risk. Nothing currently in the public record indicates Huang ever disclosed the affair or stepped aside from a single decision involving Megaspeed.
Huang’s second relationship crossed a similarly bright governance line in that it involved an executive who reported directly to him. In the past, corporate boards at McDonald’s and Intel ousted chief executives over relationships with employees, and an ally working on Huang’s return conceded , “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.”
Those lapses unfolded inside an organization seemingly engineered to leave its leader unchecked, with roughly 60 direct reports , family in senior posts, and no clear successor , board chair, or chief compliance officer . When a board of directors can no longer trust a chief executive, removal is their duty. We would argue that Huang’s conduct would be unacceptable of any chief executive, founder or not.
Nowhere did that breakdown in trust carry steeper stakes than in China, where Huang was Washington’s foremost advocate for looser export rules. Documents reviewed by Bloomberg place servers holding Nvidia's H800, H100, and H200 chips inside a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network. Some of those units reportedly went first to Aperia Cloud Services, an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in Singapore, before being smuggled into China. The servers were pledged as collateral in January 2025, when all three chips were barred from sale to China, nearly a year before President Donald Trump’s December 2025 decision — lobbied for by Huang and backed by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick—to let Nvidia sell the H200 to approved Chinese buyers for a 25% U.S. government cut.
Far more alarming, other top-tier Nvidia hardware reached a blacklisted institution with ties to China’s military , where American technology could be turned against the United States. Procurement records document A100 and H100 purchases by People’s Liberation Army units, and Reuters reports that a blacklisted defense university bought two H200s through a reseller in September. Neither source says Nvidia made the sales. Exporting controlled silicon to China’s military or blacklisted entities without a license is illegal regardless.
China’s premier AI labs built their newest models on export-controlled hardware too. Their “innovation” rests partly on American chips they were banned from buying and American models they were barred from copying. A forensic study found the fingerprint of Nvidia's Blackwell chips in six Chinese frontier models, and Anthropic says it caught Chinese labs distilling its models at massive scale—raising the question of whether their “innovation” rests partly on American chips they were banned from buying and models they were barred from copying. The study neither pinpoints where the Blackwell hardware sat nor establishes whether its use violated any law.
Even without smuggling, Chinese companies tap advanced chips in Southeast Asian data centers built expressly for them, a loophole that was legal until the Commerce Department’s recent rule . The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia told many overseas cloud partners to keep Chinese customers below a ceiling of 30% to 49%. A supplier policing that ratio knows the figure, and disclosing it would be an elementary first step toward accountability.
In May 2025, three months after Dell cut off Aperia over diversion fears, Huang insisted there was “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Yet short seller Culper Research counts billings routed through Singapore swelling from 8.5% of Nvidia's revenue to roughly 20% over three years, hitting 22% in the quarter ended July 2025. The very next quarter, the standalone Singapore line vanished from company filings when Nvidia switched to reporting sales by customer headquarters.
In financial statements, Nvidia has said that over 99% of controlled data-center revenue billed in Singapore came from US-based customers. But a buyer that books orders through a U.S. entity is not the same as an American end user. Megaspeed bought most of its hardware through Aivres, the California arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker which has been blacklisted for supporting China’s military. Suggesting that Singapore’s surging billings reflected nothing beyond American demand strains credulity.
Neither Huang nor Nvidia has been formally charged with a crime, and the company maintains it complies with the law. Where the board’s unfinished inquiry would ordinarily counsel patience, it seems clear to us that the push to restore him anyway points to the financial self-interest driving his backers.
Under Huang, Nvidia remade itself into its customers’ chief financier, “a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding,” as The New York Times phrased it. Through July, its equity stakes ballooned from about $7 billion to $99 billion. It has agreed to conditionally guarantee up to $105 billion in leases for OpenAI’s Ohio campus, and one economist calculates it backstops up to $125 billion of a $500 billion financing program with Wall Street firms.
Huang may have personally assembled this financial edifice, but the fractures were showing before the scandal broke. By August, Nvidia was negotiating billions in guarantees for buyers unable to afford its hardware outright. Colette Kress, Nvidia former finance chief and now interim CEO, halved Nvidia's initial commitment to OpenAI, and late that month the firm paused certain credit backstops for cloud operators.
Without Huang, smaller “neocloud” operators could face a painful reckoning. Nvidia's backing was widely seen as a hedge against capture by its largest customers—hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, which together account for about half its revenue.
