articles.title_orig: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.title_zh: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.
Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.
As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.
A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.
Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”
Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.
During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”
It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos , who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.
The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.
During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”
India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.
The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. On Tuesday, shares of technology companies in Asia tumbled after the Trump administration announced rules to restrict overseas access to advanced A.I. chips like those sold by Nvidia. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

articles.title_orig: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.title_zh: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services, though Chase said its issue has now been resolved.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems was behind the glitch and it was not a cyber security incident.
A spokesperson said "this was not a systemic issue" but noted the impact may have affected other banks "only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us".
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights .
In addition, United Airlines also reported a "widespread system outage".
The problems with the banks started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News, though Chase Bank told the BBC that customers still had access to their accounts and funds.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.
Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
That issue resolved within a few hours.
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.
The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.
On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.
The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
November 13, 2026 at 16:36 JST
A Taiwanese fact check institution determined that this photo, released by the Eastern Theater Command of the Chinese military on Aug. 6, 2022, is a synthetic image. (Captured from the website of China’s Ministry of National Defense)
Anime videos that have ridiculed the Japanese government’s responses to inflation, fuel shortages and natural disasters have spread online and gained overwhelming praise supposedly from Japanese citizens.
But upon further look, the videos were all created by artificial intelligence in China, part of an apparent “cognitive warfare” attack intended to promote internal strife within Japan.
And it was unclear if the Japanese responses on social media were authentic.
These videos, which featured Chinese captions, were initially posted on Chinese video sharing platform Bilibili under the same user name. They were later reposted on X.
One of them, uploaded in late August, sarcastically made light of Japan’s measures to deal with rising rice prices and shortages of naphtha.
“Empty shelves hold nothing but price tags, and signs line the aisles saying: ‘Restock: TBD,’” the caption in Chinese read. “Even the snack packages have faded to black and white, and they (Japanese government) keep insisting none of this counts as a price rise.”
The Japanese service of China Global Television Networks, a Chinese state media, reported details of the animated videos on Sept. 2.
The report, titled, “Hitting a sore spot, and hard to rebut,” emphasized that many Japanese lauded the videos with messages saying, “Genius!” “Good sense,” and “right to the point,” on social media. It said compliments far outpaced criticism.
For Chinese people, Sept. 3 was Victory over Japan Day, marking the end of the Second Sino-Japanese War.
Jun Osawa, a senior researcher at the Nakasone Peace Institute, a public interest incorporated foundation, believes the videos were used as a cognitive warfare operation to coincide with the Chinese anniversary.
“It’s a new way to fuel social anxiety and spark government criticism in Japan,” he said.
A nation or a non-state stakeholder, such as a terrorist group, conducts cognitive warfare operations to influence policy decisions of an opponent by spreading specific narratives that play on people’s emotions.
Such operations aim to create internal divisions and undermine public trust in an opponent country’s society and systems.
The Japanese government is aware of China using such a strategy, but previous efforts were aimed at influencing external opinions about Japan.
When Japan released tons of treated water from the crippled Fukushima No. 1 nuclear power plant into the ocean, China described the discharge as “nuclear-contaminated water” and pushed that concept to the world.
More recently, China has repeatedly accused Japan of turning to “neo-militarism” at international conferences and other occasions. These accusations came after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in the Diet in November 2025 that Japan could respond to a possible war in Taiwan.
The latest AI-generated videos appear designed to influence opinion within the country.
The United States and European nations consider Russia and China to be the primary operators of cognitive warfare.
According to a report from European External Action Services (EEAS), which serves as the foreign ministry of the European Union, 540 cases of “foreign information manipulation and interference” were uncovered in 2025. Of them, Russia carried out the most, with 157 cases, followed by China, with 31.
Japan was targeted in 13 cases, ranking 12th in the world, while Ukraine placed first, with 112 cases amid the war with Russia.
Cognitive warfare using AI to manipulate information has also been commonly used to affect political elections.

articles.title_orig: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.title_zh: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve’s Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve’s Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.
The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6 . Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.
President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.
“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”
In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”
Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.
The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.
The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.
Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

articles.title_orig: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.title_zh: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.content_orig:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

articles.title_orig: The Metacritic Review Score Bar For ‘GTA 6’ Is Historically High
articles.title_zh: The Metacritic Review Score Bar For ‘GTA 6’ Is Historically High
articles.content_orig:
Reviews for Grand Theft Auto 6 are on the way from a batch of critics who reportedly had a whole lot of time to play it. While some are content to ignore Metacritic review scores, millions of gamers, loads of developers and overlord publishers very, very much care about them. And GTA 6 is going to be more scrutinized than almost any other game in history in that regard.
It’s hard to overstate just how high the bar is here for GTA 6’s Metacritic score . It essentially has to be one of the best-scored games of all time to match its predecessors, and even something like a low 90 would be considered a quality underperformance by some (I would argue unfairly, but this is the reality of the industry). So, what are the past scores here?
First of all, it’s hard to believe we got four huge Grand Theft Auto games in the span of seven years, from 2001 to 2008. Boy, have times changed. Second, you can see what I mean here: every GTA game from III to V , with Vice City and San Andreas in the middle, has a 95-98 score. I think we can agree that GTA 2 is not really a part of this conversation, and it came before the franchise really blew up.
More recently, GTA IV and V have gotten a 98 and 97, respectively. GTA IV is tied with SoulCalibur and Super Mario Galaxy 2 as the second-highest-scored game of all time (No. 1 is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at a 99; the remaster currently has a 96). To put this in more context, out of 150 reviews on Xbox 360 and PS3, 75 of those are 10/10 scores.
If GTA 6 is below a 95 Metacritic score, I can guarantee you there is going to be an annoying narrative based on that. I do believe we have now entered an era of increased engagement bait and it is possible that some outlets or creators could sink it with a lower score just to stand out. Not that people have to like the game, but the last few years I have seen this happen repeatedly with other high-profile games, so keep that in mind. If someone gives GTA 6 a 5/10, that will probably be the most clicked-on review out of all of them.
Financially? No, it doesn’t matter. GTA 6 has 16 million pre-orders and over $1.5 billion in estimated revenue, and the game isn’t even out yet. It will be the fastest-selling game of all time and will try to someday surpass GTA 5 as the best-selling AAA game in history. A few Metacritic score points won’t matter. We cannot rule out the (very, very slim) possibility it may bomb, which would be a big deal, but needless to say, even if that doesn’t happen, expectations are sky-high based on the series’ history.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Said to Guide IPO Price to Top of Range or Above
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Said to Guide IPO Price to Top of Range or Above
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company is planning to close the order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and start trading on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic's IPO proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. But Anthropic is facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the U.S.
A group of researchers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code .
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus . It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its listing.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
"I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey," Amodei said.

articles.title_orig: ‘A Possible Stampede’—Fed Issues Serious Bank Run Warning As Outages Fuel Wild November 17 ‘Blackout’ Theories
articles.title_zh: ‘A Possible Stampede’—Fed Issues Serious Bank Run Warning As Outages Fuel Wild November 17 ‘Blackout’ Theories
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: Elon in, Jensen out: Trump leans on Musk during latest China visit
articles.title_zh: Elon in, Jensen out: Trump leans on Musk during latest China visit
articles.content_orig:
The president is headed this week to summits in the Philippines and China that will include a meeting with Xi Jinping and a trilateral meeting with Xi and Vladimir Putin.
President Donald Trump heads to China later this week for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on trade and denuclearization, but one topic that won’t be on Trump’s agenda, according to U.S. officials, is Nvidia.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation after an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sent political shock waves through Washington. Trump confirmed that the FBI was looking into the case, and lawmakers are demanding answers about whether China was able to access Nvidia’s advanced computer chips, which are used for artificial intelligence.
Leaving the White House Monday morning, the president said “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy” as he downplayed national security concerns. “It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China. But our country now militarily is stronger than we’ve ever been,” Trump told reporters. The president also said he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO, but added he may talk to Xi about the spying allegations.
Still, despite the growing number of questions about Nvidia, a U.S. official who previewed the president’s trip to reporters in a background call Friday said it “should not really have any bearing on the trip in all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese.”
“I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it’s probably not something that we’re going to read the Chinese in on at this moment,” the U.S. official said.
Those questions about China’s access to advanced computer chips spilled out into the public last week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not implementing stricter controls on exports of Nvidia chips to Megaspeed International, a company run by the alleged Chinese spy. Beijing has denied the espionage allegations.
The White House has expressed “complete confidence” in Lutnick, and a Department of Commerce spokesperson told MS NOW, “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions.”
“These are national security matters that we develop in the administration,” the U.S. official said on the call, adding that it was an “interagency process” and that officials “don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.” The official did say the U.S. was discussing closing “loopholes” in existing measures to control exports of advanced AI chips to China.
The president’s trip to Asia includes two international summits: first in Manila, Philippines, to meet with leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, followed by Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen, China. Accompanying the president, according to the White House are Bessent, Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett and U.S. Trade representative Jamieson Greer.
Last week Trump called Huang’s resignation a “horrible thing” and said he didn’t plan to raise the situation with the Chinese leader. But the president added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. I mean, he built a great company.”
In May, Huang accompanied Trump on a trip to China for a state visit. It was on that trip that Rubio briefed Trump about Huang’s alleged connection to a suspected Chinese spy, according to a U.S. official granted anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence information. Trump has denied that he received that warning, which was first reported by The New York Times.
A second U.S. official on Friday’s preview call told reporters that SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk was expected to accompany Trump to Asia. The U.S. official said that Musk would be traveling as an adviser given his “tremendous business interests” in the U.S.-China relationship and that he was a “big part of our national security.”
One area Trump is expected to confront Xi over is China’s growing nuclear arsenal.
Previewing a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, a second U.S. official briefing reporters on the same call said it was time for China to “step up” to the “adult table” on nuclear nonproliferation talks. While Russia and the U.S. have larger stockpiles, the official criticized China’s rapid nuclear development, adding that “things that China is doing very opaquely with their nuclear arsenals” affect the “security of every human being in the world.”
The official added that the administration was not expecting any immediate denuclearization agreement from the trilateral meeting, stressing that the occasion would serve as the “entry point” for further efforts to reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
The three leaders are also expected to discuss the war with Iran, according to the U.S. official. Both China and Russia have provided an economic lifeline to Iran through their existing trade relationships, but Trump has downplayed any significant military support to Tehran.
There are no plans for a bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin at the APEC summit. The U.S. official said the president did not plan to discuss the war in Ukraine in the trilateral meeting given separate ongoing negotiations being led by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Musk, whose Starlink system has been used in the war by Ukraine, will not attend the trilateral meeting, the U.S. official said.
Trump told reporters Monday he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The president didn’t offer any additional information other than a potential meeting would take place in China.
After visiting Beijing in May, this will be Trump’s second trip to China this year, and his third meeting with Xi in as much time. Two months ago the Chinese president visited Trump at the White House. The trilateral will be Trump’s second official meeting with the Russian president in his second term, after an Alaska summit last year.
One contentious topic the Trump administration didn’t mention in its readout from the president’s last meeting with Xi is Taiwan. Chinese officials previewing APEC and Trump’s visit stressed to MS NOW in a mid-October press briefing that they continued to oppose Taiwan’s “independence” and U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.title_zh: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.content_orig:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI, says it put public at risk by developing AI without safeguards
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI, says it put public at risk by developing AI without safeguards
articles.content_orig:
A cash cow. Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac hide caption
Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?
Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money . By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
Then Google vice president of search Marissa Mayer in 2009. ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion . That's more than a millionfold increase.
Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.
In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.
Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer , a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.
Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."
Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.
If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.
Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.
The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail .
Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.
The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.
Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?
Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages , recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go .
The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.
But they didn't release it.
Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.
Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.
So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?
Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?
His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.
In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.
Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.
"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.
Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist , sexist , and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.
And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.
Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma . Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.
Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.
We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?
Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.
The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 20 Pro Screen Protectors Show Rumored Curved Design
articles.title_zh: iPhone 20 Pro Screen Protectors Show Rumored Curved Design
articles.content_orig:
Screen protector samples circulating online offer an early look at how Apple's rumored iPhone 20 Pro redesign could look, with rounded edges that could help create the appearance of a nearly borderless display.
Sharing a video of the purported screen protector on X yesterday , the leaker known as "Ice Universe" described next year's anticipated iPhone redesign as a "milestone." In a follow-up post on Weibo today, Ice Universe added, in translation, that "the era of easy screen protector application is coming to an end. The era of a comfortable grip is approaching."
The glass illustrates several elements repeatedly described in rumors about the anniversary iPhone, including shallow curves along all four edges, rounded corners, and an extremely narrow border.
The Apple iPhone 20 Pro is going to feature a milestone design - let's take a look first https://t.co/n8uNrZgh0S
— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) November 16, 2026
The post follows a separate handheld video shared by Ice Universe on November 14, with text identifying it as an approved "3D quad-curved cover glass" sample. Similar glass pieces have been circulating since early October on Weibo and X. On October 7 , Weibo blogger "体验more" shared photographs of samples in two sizes, suggesting that they looked like concept designs based on leaked information.
The screen protectors likely represent early manufacturing tests based on rumors, rather than parts made to Apple's actual specifications. Experimental pieces allow manufacturers to explore new manufacturing techniques ahead of having access to the finished device's dimensions.
The samples also show a Dynamic Island that appears comparable to the narrower version introduced on the iPhone 18 Pro . That would suggest no further substantial reduction for the anniversary model, in line with display analyst Ross Young's prediction that the smaller ‌Dynamic Island‌ would remain through 2027.
The glass offers a physical depiction of the design direction described in earlier rumors. Ice Universe previously suggested that the anniversary iPhone would use shallow curves alongside optical refraction and other visual effects to make the display borders less visible.
That shape could also complicate screen protector designs. A protector covering the curved edges would need to follow their contours closely, making its fit dependent on the final glass geometry. Ice Universe's latest comments point to that potential tradeoff between a more rounded feel and the convenience of applying a flat protector.
The footage arrives amid an increasingly detailed picture of the 20th anniversary iPhone. Yesterday, the leaker "Fixed Focus Digital" claimed that the models would use glass similar to the iPhone Air , but with greater curvature on all four sides. Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected in the fall of 2027, although the "iPhone 20 Pro" name remains speculative.

articles.title_orig: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.title_zh: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.content_orig:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.
“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.”
Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does.
“It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.”
The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app.
NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own.
SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email.

articles.title_orig: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now
articles.title_zh: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now
articles.content_orig:
I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
As recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11 . But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop , could struggle. Microsoft was talking a big game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit , and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit .
Earlier this month , Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”
The most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.
When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri says, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”
To test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model , it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.
Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle
Before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open showed memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the update.
Now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 ( memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.
Taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.
I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.
As I said when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13 , I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.
Our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era . Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

articles.title_orig: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.title_zh: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.title_zh: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.
With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.
Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.
"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.
Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.
The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.
One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.
With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.
By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.
Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

articles.title_orig: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after running in prestigious race: "Distressing and completely unacceptable"
articles.title_zh: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after running in prestigious race: "Distressing and completely unacceptable"
articles.content_orig:
The dead body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.
Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn't be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn't been properly buried.
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in a statement. "He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred," he added. "My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been "humanely euthanized under anesthesia" after receiving emergency treatment.
"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said. "What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state's horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.
"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," he said. "We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week."
Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the landfill, told national broadcaster ABC the horse's body was moved to a permitted area of the site.
"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson told ABC. "The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons. In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.
"These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses," Racing NSW said in a statement. "The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect."
The state's racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals that have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," the statement continued. "If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."
Australian politician Emma Hurst called the news "absolutely heartbreaking," but not surprising, ABC reported.
"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said. "To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament."
